Abstract
The Paris Agreement created an institutionalized role for non-state actors through voluntary cooperation.

Many international NGOs (INGOs) are particularly active in these “Paris partnerships,” often working with multinational corporations to reduce emissions. Though there is ample work on both the effectiveness of the Paris partnerships and on the role of INGOs in the global climate regime, much of this work focuses

“outward” – on how INGOs contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation, or influence norms, discourse and policy. Yet, there is considerably less work that focuses “inward” – asking why climate INGOs act the way they do. To better understand the incentives and opportunities that drive INGO behavior, I examine their relationships with large corporations. Specifically, this paper uses a network analysis to map the relationships between Fortune100 firms and a key subset of well-resourced INGOs, whom I refer to as “the climate establishment,” through the Paris partnerships. The climate establishment can be understood as insider INGOs who work within the multilateral process and with large corporations to influence rulemaking, soft law and firm behavior. I present new social network data to provide insights into the structural incentives and constraints that these partnerships create for INGOs. These findings suggest that in addition to assessing partnership effectiveness, scholars should also consider how relationships with multinational corporations shape the climate establishment’s organizational behavior.
1. Introduction

Public-private partnerships have been a staple of the global climate regime since the late 1990s. The 2015 Paris Agreement institutionalizes a role for non-state actor cooperation through voluntary partnerships. There are currently 149 “international cooperative initiatives” (i.e. partnerships) registered with the UNFCCC, which include firms, non-governmental organizations and sub-national governments.[1]

A large and growing body of work seeks to evaluate the effects of these partnerships. This research can largely be divided into two strands: evaluating emissions reductions of these initiatives and conceptualizing indirect pathways to decarbonization that these partnerships may catalyze. But before asking whether the Paris partnerships are an effective approach to meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement, it is helpful to examine how these voluntary collaborations may affect individual organizational behavior. The incentives, goals and behavior of individual organizations will have a direct bearing on partnership performance.

The Paris Agreement identifies non-Party stakeholders, including international INGOs, as key sources for mitigation and adaptation activities. In this “all hands on deck approach,” INGOs provide expertise, implementation know-how, and legitimacy for multi-actor partnerships (Hale 2016). Many of these INGOs are well-resourced, highly professionalized organizations whom I refer to as the “climate establishment”

– insiders working within the multilateral process and cooperating with multinational corporations to influence rulemaking, soft law and firm behavior. I borrow from Bush’s concept of the “democracy establishment” – which she defines as professional organizations whose U.S.-funded democracy
assistance programs fail to challenge the political conditions that allow dictators to obtain and hold power (Bush 2016).

The analogous group in climate policy are professional environmentalists. Though they do not all hold identical beliefs about pathways to decarbonization, they share common characteristics: they are highly educated experts who generally advocate a moderate approach to climate policy (Skocpol 2013; Huber 2022). They participate actively in UNFCCC negotiations, demonstrating their belief that cooperation on emissions mitigation is critical to addressing climate change. And they partner with large corporations in the hopes of advancing decarbonization.

To supplement the extant, and often inconclusive, research on the mitigation potential of the Paris partnerships, this paper shifts the unit of analysis from the partnership to the organizational level in order to understand the incentives of INGOs that comprise the climate establishment. While partnerships can potentially accelerate decarbonization, they may also undermine environmental INGOs’ ability to be effective advocates for change. Insights from the study of transnational networks and social network analysis suggest that ties between organizations can influence organizational goals and strategies (Granovetter 1985; Keck and Sikkink 1998; Hadden 2015). I argue that the ties between the climate establishment and Fortune 100 firms are an important scope condition that influences the potential effectiveness of the Paris partnerships. Though traditionally viewed as the vanguard for climate policy, the climate establishment faces organizational constraints that may limit its ability to be as effective advocates for decarbonization.

The paper proceeds as follows. First, I review the literatures on the role of international NGOs in the climate regime and social networks in international relations. Together, these two literatures illustrate why network ties are a key factor in understanding the effects of the Paris partnerships. Next, I provide descriptive data on the climate establishment and its relationships to Fortune 100 companies. Finally, I discuss the implications of these networks, showing how links to the private sector can constrain the strategies and behavior of the climate establishment.
2. Literature Review
The challenges of evaluating partnership effectiveness

The Paris Agreement has ushered in a new era of non-state actor participation in the climate regime. The UNFCCC decision adopting the Paris Agreement “encourages Parties to work closely with non-Party stakeholders to catalyze efforts to strengthen mitigation and adaptation action” through voluntary initiatives, and creates an institutional infrastructure to support these efforts (UNFCCC 2016, paras. 118; 121–22). As Hale notes, this new “catalytic and facilitative” model views non-state actors (including INGOs) as “a core element of its logic of spurring rising action on climate over time” (Hale 2016, p. 14).

The 149 partnerships undertake a variety of activities – some of which preceded the Paris Agreement and were subsequently registered with the UNFCCC. For example, the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil,

created in 2004, seeks to reduce the social, environmental and climate impacts of palm oil production through a certification scheme. A collaborative effort between governments, INGOs and firms, the RSPO estimates that 1.8 Mt of CO2 emissions have been avoided as a result of its efforts.[2]

Evaluating the effects of these partnerships is crucial to understanding whether and how they are contributing to the goals of the Paris Agreement.(Hsu et al. 2019) However, the empirical record of these activities is unclear. This is partially because some of these partnerships are relatively new, and it may take time to see the results. Yet, it is also due to the inherent challenges of evaluating their effects. How much will they abate (and based on what assumptions)? Is it plausible that these reductions are double counted – by both partnership members and governments? What are the indirect effects of voluntary cooperation, and how can policymakers and participants evaluate their indirect effects?

It is true that these partnerships could be an important addition to climate governance, and theories of systemic change support this view.(Hale 2020; Sabel and Victor 2022) However, in reality we know little about their ability to achieve decarbonization. There is a large literature that seeks to quantify the potential emissions contributions of the Paris partnerships (Hsueh 2017; Hsu et al. 2018; Roelfsema et al. 2018; Kuramochi et al. 2020; Lui et al. 2021; Hale et al. 2021), but these works suffer from two main shortcomings.

First, estimating emissions reductions presents a number of challenges – including breadth of analysis, underlying assumptions, and potential for double counting. For example, a study by Lui et al. only estimates the contributions of 17 partnerships with the explicit selection criteria that the partnership must potentially mitigate hundreds of millions of tons of CO2e (Lui et al. 2021). However, estimates of many partnerships indicate that their mitigative potential pales in comparison to the overall challenges of rapid decarbonization.(UN Environment Programme 2018, chap. 5). Others assume that partnerships will meet their targets, and/or that they will continue to expand (New Climate Institute et al. 2021, app. 1).

In addition, the potential for double counting makes accurate estimation of potential mitigation effects more challenging. One study suggests that there may be up to 80% overlap between reduction estimates of countries’ national pledges (i.e. Nationally Determined Contributions) and the Paris partnerships

(Roelfsema et al. 2018). In other words, it is difficult to ascertain whether governments have incorporated some of the partnerships activities in their own NDCs. Thus, estimates of partnerships’ mitigative impact vary widely (Kuramochi et al. 2020; Hsu et al. 2020; Lui et al. 2021; New Climate Institute et al. 2021). Finally, it is worth reiterating that because of the nature of the voluntary approach, all data on progress are self-reported, creating further challenges for accurate data.

A second task for understanding the impacts of the Paris partnerships is conceptualizing and evaluating indirect effects. Scholars of decarbonization point to how learning, experimentation and first-mover leadership can help catalyze larger changes (Green 2014; Hale 2020; Sabel and Victor 2022). These indirect effects may contribute to decarbonization in the long run, but are hard to conceptualize, let alone measure (van der Ven et al. 2016). For example, in addition to requiring members to develop and share

climate plans, the C40 Cities partnership provides a platform for city governments to share research and best practices on climate policy. The Climate Smart Agriculture Booster aims to “pioneer the transition to climate-smart agriculture across Europe and around the world” by providing a platform for participating governments, firms and INGOs to share knowledge, capacity building tools, technical assistance and other resources to promote climate smart agriculture.[3] Information sharing is a hallmark of many Paris partnerships, and global governance networks more generally (Sikkink 2009). Yet, these two examples both illustrate that many effects – such as knowledge and capacity building – are not readily quantified (Hsu et al. 2019).

Instead of wrestling with the difficulties of measuring outcomes, both direct and indirect, I shift the unit of analysis to the organizational level, using social network analysis (SNA). SNA provides insights into how partnerships create material and political incentives for the climate establishment. By mapping the structure of the network and the position of INGOs therein, this study seeks to understand the scope conditions for partnership effectiveness, to understand whether the most progressive actors participating in the Paris partnerships have the incentives to push for ambitious action.

Social networks are one way to understand patterns of authority and how new forms of governance emerge and operate (Kahler 2009, p. 3). SNA can be particularly useful in the study of non-state actors, where less formalized modes of authority are more common (Eilstrup-Sangiovanni 2017). While network analysis cannot assess the effectiveness of the Paris partnerships, it can identify which members of the climate establishment enjoy positions of authority through their ties with each other, and with F100 firms.

Connections can provide opportunities, material resources, ideas and strategies. For example, NGOs with central positions in transnational advocacy networks can serve as “gatekeepers,” shaping which issues get adopted by the larger network (Carpenter 2007; Carpenter et al. 2014). Network centrality can also translate to greater authority for private rulemakers: as a greater number of actors recognize and replicate private rules from a given organization, the organization’s regulatory reach expands (Green 2013). Ties can be the source of new ideas, as Hadden shows in her study of transnational climate advocacy networks (Hadden 2015). NGOs that emphasized science were more likely to adopt contentious tactics when participating in meetings and events with NGOs that did the same. Moreover, central actors in a social network can be an engine of norm emergence, planting a “seed” which then spreads through a small number of key actors to the larger network (Lake and Wong 2009, p. 135). Finally, and critically for this study, network ties are a two-way street. They provide both opportunities for influence as well as limits on autonomy (Hafner-Burton et al. 2009).
3. Data and Methods

I focus on the climate establishment because it is often perceived as an important engine of change in the global climate regime (Newell 2000; Betsill and Corell 2008; Green 2014). There is a long history of climate NGOs sounding alarms, holding governments accountable, advocating for more ambitious action and making moral arguments to justify that action (e.g. Raustiala 1997; Newell 2000; Betsill and Corell
2008). Of all the actors involved in the Paris Agreement, it is reasonable to assume that the climate establishment would be among the most progressive. NGOs are viewed as “the conscience of the

world,”(Willetts 1996) imbued with a desire for change, and free of many of the political and material constraints faced by governments and the private sector. If the Paris partnerships are to contribute to achieving the goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, it is reasonable to assume that the climate establishment will serve a key role.

To understand the organizational incentives of the climate establishment, I examine its cooperation with large emitters through joint memberships in voluntary partnerships. The UNFCCC’s Global Climate Action Portal serves as a clearinghouse for voluntary climate efforts by non-state actors, including “International Cooperative Initiatives” (ICIs) which have multiple members. I investigate these cooperative initiatives to ascertain which environmental INGOs constitute the climate establishment, per their decision to cooperate with F100 companies.

INGOs that comprise the climate establishment must meet two criteria. First, they must be in the top 10th percentile of total delegates sent to the UNFCCC annual Conference of the Party meetings (COP). I build on Allan’s data (2020) which tracks NGO participation in the COP meetings from 1995 to 2015, when the
Paris Agreement was signed. Appendix 1 provides details on this coding process.

The total number of delegates is a proxy for INGOs’ capacity and thus, their potential to influence policy. Larger, more professionalized organizations can send more people to conferences. More representation, operationalized as larger delegations at conferences, captures organizational ability to influence others

(Orsini 2013). Following Stroup and Wong, I refer to these as “leading INGOs:” high profile organizations that receive deference from multiple audiences – from governments to corporations to the media (2017). This includes business NGOs, universities and think-tanks with the largest number of delegates sent to the COPs between 1995 and 2015. (For a list of all leading INGOs, see Table A1.)
But the climate establishment organizations are not simply those with the most delegates at the COPs;

they must also cooperate with large emitters via joint membership in a Paris partnership. Fortune 100 companies serve as a proxy for large emitters. These firms own or derive revenue from large “climateforcing” assets (Colgan, Green, and Hale 2021). These are a diverse group of firms, which includes banks, insurance, communications, technology and fossil fuel companies among others. Not all of these firms generate large direct emissions, yet they all have or contribute to significant GHG emissions. For example, banks and other financial institutions have relatively small carbon footprints, but they provide financing for fossil fuel projects.

I employ social network analysis (SNA) to investigate the relationships between the climate establishment and its F100 partners. SNA is commonly used in international relations and environmental politics to understand patterns of authority (Hafner-Burton et al. 2009; Kahler 2009; Green 2013, 2022; Hadden 2015). The network analysis identifies which of the leading environmental INGOs cooperate with F100 firms through shared membership in partnerships.

The partnership data was downloaded from the Climate Initiatives Platform.[4] 245 initiatives were listed at the time of download in October 2021. Most initiatives included information on participants; these were then searched for Fortune 100 members. Of the 245 initiatives, 80 had one or more F100 firm as a member (13 were eliminated from the sample because subsequent searching revealed no participating firms.) Of these 80, 33 (41%) also had one or more environmental INGOs as members. These environmental INGOs represent the climate establishment (see Table 1), since they are cooperating with
F100 firms through shared membership in a given UNFCCC partnership.

Figure 1 illustrates the entire network – that is, all of the leading INGOs as well as Fortune 100 firms that participate in the Paris partnerships. Blue nodes are the climate establishment INGOs. Yellow nodes are other leading INGOs. Red nodes are F100 firms. Shared membership in a partnership – the line between two nodes – is evidence of cooperation, since both sets of actors agree to undertake the same activity or orient their behavior toward a specific goal. Node size corresponds to the degree centrality of each organization – i.e. the number of connections to other organizations.

Figure 1 shows that there are a number of non-environmental leading INGOs active in the Paris Partnerships. The World Business Council on Sustainable Development (WBCSD) is a business-oriented INGO that seeks to promote sustainability and climate action among its members. It is the third most central INGO in the network, after WWF and the World Resources Institute. The University of California and Yale are also big cooperators, with high degree centrality and eigenvector centrality scores, indicating not only lots of connections (degree), but connections to other important actors (eigenvector). (See Table A2 for centrality scores.)

Figure 2 limits the network to the climate establishment and F100 firms (rather than the larger sample of all leading INGOs). Bigger nodes have higher degree centrality, indicating membership in more partnerships – i.e., these organizations are bigger cooperators. Though technically a think-tank, I include the World Resources Institute (WRI), because it participates in more partnerships (N=17) than any other INGO in the entire sample. Moreover, WRI has had a critical impact on the development of firm-level carbon accounting, and thus is an important actor in the larger landscape of working with firms.(Green 2014b)

There are several key takeaways from Figures 1 and 2. First, leading INGOs include a number of business-oriented INGOs such as the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), the World Business Council on Sustainable Development and The Climate Group. Business NGOs constitute 29% of all leading INGO delegates, whereas environmental NGOs are 36%. (See Figure A1.) The considerable presence of business INGOs underscores the need for strong environmental advocacy as a potential counterbalance.

Second, in general, firms are more connected than the climate establishment. The firm average degree centrality score is 70, with a standard deviation 44.6. By contrast, the average degree centrality score for the climate establishment is 50, with a standard deviation of 52.5, indicating a non-normal distribution, as illustrated in Figure 3.

Third, the distribution of all three centrality scores clearly illustrates the powerful positions of WRI and WWF within the climate establishment. The views, tactics and strategies of these two organizations are therefore extremely important in shaping the overall influence of leading INGOs in the Paris partnerships.

Environmental Defense, the Nature Conservancy and the Sierra Club also have some centrality scores above the mean (scores normalized for comparison), indicating that they are also key players in the climate establishment.
5. Discussion

There is considerable optimism that the Paris partnerships can help catalyze big changes (Hsu et al. 2015; Hale 2020; Teunissen and Chan 2023). However, ultimately, such changes depend in part on the climate establishment’s ability to advocate for ambition, as well as the opportunities and constraints they face (Kahler 2009; Borgatti et al. 2013).

Network ties to the F100 can create serious constraints on the climate establishment’s ability to be effective advocates for aggressive action within the partnerships. First, material concerns can push the climate establishment to moderate its views and actions. Scholars have detailed how NGOs temper their political ambitions to secure funding. As a result, leading INGOs seek out “vanilla victories” – policy changes that are widely palatable but yield only incremental improvements”(Stroup and Wong 2017, p. 3). These allow INGOs to demonstrate their success, while not upsetting any of their multiple audiences by taking radical action.

Second, there are operational constraints, which encourage the climate establishment to promote shallow cooperation. Limited by the need to satisfy multiple audiences – states, corporations, donors, and peer NGOs, (Stroup and Wong 2017) the climate establishment must choose activities that does not jeopardize their authority with these audiences. Many NGOs are now large international organizations with multi-million dollar budgets, and as such are “subject to the all the pathologies common to large bureaucracies”(Gourevitch and Lake 2012, p. 4). This often leads to shallow cooperation that emphasizes process over outcome (Gourevitch and Lake 2012).

Third, there are ideological constraints. Though they are not-for-profit organizations, staff of the climate establishment is part of the professional managerial class: “salaried mental workers who do not own the means of production and whose major function can be described broadly as the reproduction of capitalist culture and capitalist class relations” (Ehrenreich and Ehrenreich 1977, p. 7. See also (Harvey
2007). Thus, they benefit materially from promoting policies that preserve and expand their organization’s funding, relevance and authority – even if this includes cooperating with big polluters.

Given these constraints, the prominent position of fossil fuel companies in the network raises questions about the degree to which cooperating members of the climate establishment can promote ambitious action. The network analysis indicates that INGOs in the climate establishment regularly partner with Royal Dutch Shell, Total, Petrobras and Exxon. Yet, social science research demonstrates that at best, many oil and gas firms favor the status quo; at worst, they seek to obstruct decarbonization (Supran and

Oreskes 2017a; Franta 2018; Vormedal et al. 2020; Franta 2021; Williams et al. 2022; Brulle 2023). More recently, fossil fuel companies have engaged in both greenwashing and “greenhushing”[5] – with little to no reporting on progress toward previously-set goals.

Yet, legacies of obstructionism have not deterred the climate establishment from cooperating with the fossil fuel industry. Exxon – arguably the biggest “bad guy” among fossil fuel companies – partners with almost half of INGOs in the climate establishment, including Conservation International, Greenpeace, Oxfam, WWF and WRI (Supran and Oreskes 2017). This is consistent with recent reporting that leading INGOs including WWF accept funding from foundations with significant fossil fuel investments.[6]

Similarly, large banks, responsible for financing the fossil fuel industry, are linked to the climate establishment. A study by a consortium of NGOs finds that the world’s 60 largest banks have provided $4.6 trillion in financing to fossil fuel projects since the adoption of the Paris Agreement in 2015.[7] Fully three-quarters of the “dirty dozen” identified in the report – those banks providing the most fossil fuel

financing – also participate in Paris partnerships. And three-quarters of the climate establishment are cooperating with one or more members of this “dirty dozen” through partnerships such as the Climate Ambition Alliance: Net Zero 2050, Cities Climate Finance Leadership Alliance, and the Carbon Pricing Leadership Coalition.

Finally, Table 2 shows that all top five cooperators of the climate establishment participate in at least one of three carbon pricing partnerships: The Carbon Pricing Leadership Coalition (CPLC), Business Leadership Criteria on Carbon Pricing (BLCC) and the Climate, Community and Biodiversity Alliance (CCBA). The CPLC seeks to expand the use of carbon pricing internationally. It is also the third largest partnership in terms of climate establishment and F100 participants, illustrating that it is widely viewed as an important approach to emissions mitigation. The BLCC encourages firms to price carbon internally. Finally, the CCBA is used as a “tag” for voluntary carbon offsets – indicating which projects have met their criteria for social responsibility and biodiversity. The data indicate that carbon pricing is clearly a key strategy for the climate establishment.

However, carbon pricing has a very mixed track record – both politically and in terms of its effects on emissions. It often creates considerable political backlash (Mildenberger and Stokes 2020), which is not necessarily allayed by revenue recycling (Mildenberger et al. 2022). Most carbon pricing policies encourage efficiency or fuel-switching rather than real progress toward decarbonization (Green 2021) More importantly, however, carbon pricing is increasingly supported by the oil and gas industry, indicating that they view potential gains from the expanded use of carbon pricing.(Vormedal et al. 2020).

Indeed, almost all the fossil fuel companies in the sample participate in at least one carbon pricing partnership. Utilities and energy companies, which also have a track record of climate obstructionism (Stokes 2020; Williams et al. 2022), are also active participants.

There are, of course, limits to this analysis. It is reasonable to argue that there is a selection effect operating in these networks: the climate establishment cooperates with F100 firms because it views cooperation with polluters as a source for solutions. However, insights from social science and network analysis suggest that there are reasons that this model of policy change may not reflect reality. The ties between these two groups indicates that the climate establishment is exposed to organizational incentives not to advocate for greater ambition.

Finally, it is important to note that though the climate establishment cooperates with large corporations through the Paris partnerships, it may also engage in more confrontational approaches such as protest or direct action. Examining these other tactics is beyond the scope of this study.
6. Conclusion and Future Research

Partnerships are a key part of the Paris Agreement. Yet it is notoriously difficult to estimate the emissions reductions, much less the indirect effects, of these voluntary efforts. Instead of measuring outcomes, I examine the relationships among the climate establishment and Fortune 100 firms to understand who cooperates via joint membership in these partnerships. The network analysis shows that the climate establishment is cooperating with many large emitters, some of which are known climate obstructionists.

Second, it also participates in many carbon pricing initiatives, which have limited effects on emissions reductions. Finally, insights from social network analysis suggest there are multiple pathways through which ties to large corporations can constrain the climate establishment’s ability to advocate for deep decarbonization.

Future research should examine the extent to which the climate establishment engages in other approaches to decarbonization. When do they choose to cooperate with large emitters, and when do they choose more confrontational approaches? To what extent do these organizations also see restricting the supply of fossil fuels as an important part of their advocacy portfolio? Understanding the motivations of the climate establishment will yield greater insights into the potential effectiveness of the Paris partnerships, particularly given the challenges of measuring their emissions reductions.
